title: The Spice Islands — The Age of Exploration, Chapter 1
eyebrow: CKHG Grade 5 · The Age of Exploration · Chapter 1 · Student Reader pp. 2–9
bigQuestion: According to the author, how did the search for the Spice Islands change history?

missions.name: The Spice Islands
missions.blurb: One quiz for the whole chapter. Every highlighted word in the chapter is in here — what it means on one paper, what it is doing in the chapter on the other. The card says which page answers it, and a wrong answer opens that page.

hi: but also as a way to preserve it

vs.q: Besides adding flavor, what did medieval Europeans need spices for?
opts: Keeping food from going rotten before it was eaten
Making the cloth dyes that colored their clothes
Keeping away the diseases that spread in the towns
Feeding the animals kept through the winter months
vs.why: There was no refrigeration of any kind, so food had to be preserved some other way. That is why spices were worth so much trouble: not taste, but keeping meat safe to eat.

vs.q: This chapter is set in medieval Europe. What does medieval mean?
opts: Relating to the Middle Ages in Europe
Living in the countryside rather than a town
Belonging to a time before anyone could write
Having to do with ships and sailing
vs.why: The Middle Ages, roughly the 400s to the 1400s. The word is in the chapter's first sentence because everything in the chapter depends on this being a time with no way to keep food cold.

vs.q: The chapter says spices were very expensive. Why?
opts: They grew in faraway Asia, and the trip was dangerous
The plants had almost died out and were nearly gone
European rulers put a heavy tax on every spice sold
Only a few cooks in Europe knew how to use them
vs.why: Distance and danger, not scarcity of the plants. The spices grew in quantity — they were simply a long and risky journey away, and everything that journey cost ended up in the price.

vs.q: What does the author say Europe's wish for cheaper spices set off?
opts: The Age of Exploration and the settling of the Americas
The building of the first ships that could cross oceans
A long war between Venice and the Arab traders
The end of the Middle Ages across Europe
vs.why: This is the Big Question in one sentence. Wanting the same spices for less money is what sent Europeans out across the oceans, and the author traces the settling of the Americas back to it.

opts: In present-day Indonesia, in Southeast Asia
Off the western coast of Africa
In the Caribbean Sea, west of the Atlantic
Along the southern coast of India
vs.why: Indonesia, on the far side of Asia from Europe. Everything else in the chapter follows from how far away that is.

vs.q: The book calls Indonesia an archipelago. What is an archipelago?
opts: A chain of islands
A sea that is almost closed in by land
A country made up of many languages
A long stretch of coast with no harbors
vs.why: A chain of islands. The one the chapter means is the Malay Archipelago, which runs from the Malay Peninsula down to Australia and holds more than thirteen thousand islands — the Spice Islands being a few of them.

opts: The protected side of a mountain, which gets less rain
A cloud that sits over an island without raining
The time of year when no rain falls at all
The shade cast by the forest on a mountain slope
vs.why: Rain falls on the side of the mountain the weather hits, and the far side sits in its shadow. These islands get as much as 320 inches a year on the forested slopes and under twenty on the rain shadow sides.

vs.q: Why do the Spice Islands grow such exceptional spice crops?
opts: Heat, heavy rainfall, and rich soil
Cool nights and a long dry season
Gentle rain spread evenly all year
Sandy soil that drains after every storm
vs.why: Three things together, and the chapter names all three. It is why these particular islands were worth crossing the world for rather than any others.

vs.q: The book says European navigational skills were not up to the voyage. What does navigational mean?
opts: Related to steering and controlling a ship
Related to drawing maps of the coastline
Related to loading cargo into a ship
Related to repairing a damaged ship
vs.why: Controlling where a ship goes. The chapter uses the word to explain why Europeans could not simply go and fetch the spices themselves: they did not yet know how to steer a ship that far.

vs.q: Why could Europeans not simply sail to the Spice Islands themselves?
opts: Their ships and skills could not make such a voyage
The Arabs guarded the sea route with warships
Their rulers had forbidden such long voyages
They had no way to pay for such a long voyage
vs.why: Two things were missing, not one: ships built for the distance, and the skill to navigate it. They also did not yet know the Atlantic reached as far south as the tip of Africa.

items.hi: preserve their monopoly of the spice trade

opts: Complete control of the supply of a good
A tax charged on goods brought into a country
An agreement to share a trade between two countries
A place where people come to buy and sell goods
vs.why: Complete control of the supply. The last answer is a trading center, a different word from this same chapter — worth keeping apart, because trading centers were how the Arab traders held their monopoly.

vs.q: Arab traders told stories of monsters guarding the islands. How did that keep their monopoly?
opts: If nobody dared go, nobody else could supply spices
It frightened the Venetians into paying more
It explained to buyers why spices cost so much
It kept their own sailors from leaving them
vs.why: A monopoly lasts only while nobody else can reach the supply. For three hundred years the stories, and the secret location, did that job.

vs.q: The book says Arab traders sailed to trading centers. What is a trading center?
opts: A place where people buy and sell goods
A ship built to carry goods long distances
A tax office at the edge of a country
A storehouse where spices are kept dry
vs.why: A place where buying and selling happen. The chapter names three that the Arab traders sailed east to: India, Ceylon, and the Spice Islands themselves.

vs.q: How did spices get from the islands to Europe?
opts: Arab traders carried them west and sold them to Venetians
Venetian merchants sailed east and bought them at the islands
European ships rounded Africa and collected them yearly
Mongol riders carried them overland the whole way
vs.why: Two separate journeys, and two separate sets of people taking a profit. No European ship had yet gone round Africa, so no European bought at the source.

items.hi: negotiated with Arab traders to distribute spices

vs.q: The chapter calls the Arabs traders and the Venetians merchants. Which is right?
opts: The Arabs were the traders and the Venetians the merchants
The Venetians were the traders and the Arabs the merchants
Both words are used for the Arabs only
Both words are used for the Venetians only
vs.why: Both words mean somebody who buys and sells, and the chapter gives one to each end of the route: Arab traders brought the spices as far as Egypt, and Venetian merchants took them on into Europe.

vs.q: The Venetians negotiated with the Arab traders. What does negotiate mean?
opts: To discuss the terms of an agreement
To carry goods from one port to another
To pay a price without arguing
To lend money at a high rate
vs.why: To talk terms. What the Venetians negotiated for was the right to distribute the spices through Europe, which is what let them charge whatever they pleased.

vs.q: Kublai Khan sent Marco Polo on diplomatic missions. What is a diplomatic mission?
opts: A trip to represent your government abroad
A trip made to carry letters to a king
A journey made to trade for spices
A voyage to map an unknown coast
vs.why: Going somewhere as your government's representative. It is why Polo saw so much of Asia: the Khan kept sending him across the empire, and he paid attention everywhere he went.

vs.q: What did adventurers travel into Mongol-controlled Asia to trade for?
opts: Silk, gems, porcelain, and tea
Gold, salt, ivory, and cloth
Spices, timber, and glass
Wool, wine, and silver
vs.why: Porcelain is fine pottery, and it travelled with silk, gems and tea. The Mongols had made the roads safe, so Asia was suddenly worth the journey — and spices were not the only thing Europe wanted from it.

why.title: Why spices mattered so much
vocab: relating to the Middle Ages in Europe
a plant used to add flavor to food
text: Supermarkets today stock all sorts of spices that can be used to season or add flavor to different foods. In medieval Europe, however, people relied on spices not only to flavor their food, but also as a way to preserve it.
Without refrigerators or other cold storage, medieval Europeans used spices to extend the time period during which meats and other foods could be stored and then safely eaten before turning rotten.

cost.title: Hard to get, and so very expensive
text: In the Middle Ages, spices were hard to get. Pepper, cinnamon, ginger, cloves, and other seasonings were grown in faraway Asia.
Getting the spices to Europe took a lot of time and effort. Distances were great, and travel back and forth was dangerous. As a result, spices were very expensive.
Europe's desire for cheaper spices sparked the Age of European Exploration and its settlement of the Americas.

islands.title: Where the Spice Islands are
text: Different spices come from different places. Many of the most desirable spices come from the islands of present-day Indonesia.

Indonesia is an archipelago , or chain of islands. It stretches from Southeast Asia's Malay Peninsula to the continent of Australia. This group, known as the Malay Archipelago, contains more than thirteen thousand islands.

fire.title: Rain on one side, and very good spices
vocab: an area that gets less rain because it is on the protected side of a mountain
text: Daytime temperatures are between 70 and 90 F year-round. Rainfall can be as much as 320 inches a year on the forested mountain slopes. On the rain shadow sides, it can be less than twenty inches a year.
Heat, heavy rainfall, and rich soil result in exceptional spice crops.

secret.title: A secret worth guarding
vocab: related to controlling the movement of a ship
a person who buys and sells goods
a situation in which one person, country, or company has complete control of the supply of a good or service
a place where people buy and sell goods
text: They did not yet know that the Atlantic Ocean went as far as the southern tip of Africa. Nor were their ships and navigational skills suited to such long voyages. And at the time, the exact location of the Spice Islands was a closely guarded secret.

For hundreds of years, from around 1100 until 1400, the Arabs managed to keep the location of the Spice Islands a secret. They even made up stories about how dangerous it was to sail to these islands.

If you had been alive then you might have heard tales told by Arab traders of the fantastic monsters and hideous flesh-eating birds that guarded the Spice Islands. Stories like these were designed to help the Arab traders preserve their monopoly of the spice trade.

route.title: How the spice trade worked
vocab: a person who buys and sells goods to earn money
text: How did the spice trade work? Arab traders sailed east to trading centers in India, Ceylon (now Sri Lanka), and the Spice Islands. After loading up their ships, they sailed west again.

A typical trip took them around the Arabian Peninsula, into the Red Sea, and north to Egypt. There they sold the spices to merchants from Venice and other parts of Italy. The Arab traders made huge profits from this exchange.

venice.title: Why Venice grew rich, and disliked
vocab: to discuss the terms of an agreement
text: The Venetians did well, too. They negotiated with Arab traders to distribute spices throughout Europe. Europeans wanting to purchase spices had to deal with Venice.
Once they had acquired the spices, the Venetian merchants could set whatever prices and taxes they pleased. This arrangement made Venice a very wealthy city. It also made the Venetians unpopular.

polo.title: Into Mongol Asia
vocab: a native of the Asian nation of Mongolia
a group of people who serve as representatives of their government in another country
text: At the time, the Mongols controlled much of Asia and part of Europe. The Mongols made the roads safe for travelers, and many adventurers were anxious to seek their fortunes. Some went to trade for silk, gems, porcelain , and tea.
Kublai Khan took a liking to Marco. He sent Marco to distant parts of his kingdom on diplomatic missions . Wherever he went, Marco observed, asked questions, and remembered what he had seen.
